text: Theorem 1 proves that any quantum-inspired classical (QIC) algorithm for solving well-conditioned, sparse linear systems requires Ω(n^{1/12}) queries, while the corresponding quantum algorithm runs in poly(ln n) time, establishing the first exponential separation between the two (Theorem 1).
The quantum upper bound for sparse linear systems scales as poly(s, κ, ln(1/ε), ln n), where s is sparsity and κ is the condition number (Equation 1).
The proof reduces hardness of the QIC lower bound to a random walk oracle game on two binary trees, building on the construction of Childs et al. (Theorem 2, Section 2.1).

Lemma 2 shows the solution component corresponding to the target root vertex satisfies x_i^2 = Ω(n^{-5}||x||^2), which is what enables efficient quantum sampling but not efficient QIC sampling (Lemma 2).

The result demonstrates that quantum machine learning speedups on natural tasks are not universally reproducible by quantum-inspired classical algorithms, resolving an open question in the dequantization literature (Section 1).
